Sessions.Title: From Idea to Implementation: How AI Helped Build a Districtwide Professional Learning Ecosystem
Sessions.Short Title: A Districtwide PL Ecosystem, Built with AI
Sessions.Audience: Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Personalization & differentiation; Tool showcase
Sessions.Description:
What if AI could help school leaders do more than draft emails, summarize documents, or generate lesson plans? In this session, participants will see how AI became a design and development partner in moving an idea for reimagining professional learning into a functioning districtwide system.

The project began with a simple challenge: professional learning should not be limited to designated PD days. Educators should be able to access meaningful learning when they need it, pursue topics connected to their students and practice, and have opportunities to try, reflect, and learn from one another. From that idea came Learning in Action, a digital professional learning ecosystem that brings together on-demand learning toolkits, monthly learning challenges, learning labs, instructional coaching, curated resources, reflection, PD credit, and digital badges.

Participants will get a behind-the-scenes look at the process from initial idea to districtwide launch. The session will demonstrate how AI supported brainstorming and problem-solving, content and resource development, user-experience design, coding and troubleshooting, workflow automation, and continuous iteration. Participants will also see the places where human leadership remained essential: defining the problem worth solving, keeping students and learning at the center, protecting educator choice, making decisions about implementation, and ensuring the technology served the vision—not the other way around.

This is not a coding session. It is a practical exploration of what becomes possible when educators and leaders begin using AI not simply to complete individual tasks, but as a thought partner, builder, and capacity multiplier.

Participants will leave with a replicable problem → idea → prototype → feedback → implementation framework, a look inside the completed Learning in Action system, and concrete ideas for using AI to turn problems of practice in their own schools and districts into solutions.

No coding experience required, just a problem worth solving.

Sessions.Title: Vibe Coding for Administrators (Comp Sci Degree Not Required)

Sessions.Strands: Efficiency & productivity
Sessions.Lead Organization: Northern Valley Regional High School District
Sessions.Description:
You don't need to be a programmer to build the tools your district needs. You need to be able to identify a problem, describe it clearly, and let AI handle the rest.

I'll share tools I've built for my district using conversational AI: approval workflow systems, a scheduling conflict checker, a PII redaction tool that works offline, and a tool for verifying NJ SLEDS data.

One of the most useful things AI can build for you is a tool that runs entirely offline with no internet connection, ensuring that sensitive data never leaves your computer.

I will share the actual prompts behind tools I created, what I asked for, where the first version fell short, and how I pushed back until it worked.

No coding experience required.

Sessions.Title: Use It. Question It. Teach It: Preserving Human Thought in the Age of AI
Sessions.Short Title: Use It. Question It. Teach It.
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Efficiency & productivity; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Description:
Artificial Intelligence can instantly write, plan, summarize, differentiate, and solve. But just because AI can take over a task does not mean it should. As educators, we urge our students to embrace productive struggle and critical thinking, yet we now rely on a tool designed to eliminate intellectual friction altogether. This creates a profound paradox: In a world where technology can think with us, how do we ensure we keep thinking for ourselves?
This interactive 40 minute summit session moves far beyond basic prompt engineering to tackle the central challenge facing modern education. Grounded in cognitive science, this session introduces a simple, three part framework to help you navigate AI with intention and professional judgment:
 USE IT: Leverage AI as a true thought partner to eliminate administrative friction without sacrificing your pedagogical craft.
 QUESTION IT: Apply the Human Work Test to audit what mental effort we are outsourcing, examining accuracy, ethics, privacy, and environmental costs.
 TEACH IT: Shift from teaching students how to prompt to teaching them how to think when AI is always available.
Rather than just listening to a talk, you will engage in live Stop and Think reflection pauses, test your own place on the AI Dependency Spectrum, and leave with a turnkey, 15 minute classroom experiment that proves to students why active human effort still wins.
Whether you are an AI novice or an experienced user, you will leave with a fresh pedagogical compass and actionable strategies for your school. The ultimate goal is not to keep AI out of education, it is to keep human thought at the heart of learning. Join us to discover how.

Sessions.Title: Meet Your New Data Analyst: Gemini Notebook
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents

Sessions.Description:
School administrators are often overwhelmed by data compliance, leaving little time for strategic analysis. In this session, we introduce Gemini Notebook, Google’s secure, source-grounded AI assistant designed to turn your district's raw documents into instant, actionable insights.

Unlike standard AI chatbots, Gemini Notebok operates in a private "walled garden," generating answers based only on the documents you provide. To demonstrate its practical value for district leadership, we will walk through a real-world case study: using Gemini Notebook to analyze our school report card data. Attendees will see exactly how we leveraged this tool to rapidly synthesize dense datasets to:

-Identify hidden longitudinal trends across student demographics.
-Clearly articulate our instructional strengths for community stakeholders.
-Pinpoint specific weaknesses to guide real-time, targeted interventions.

Sessions.Title: You Can Build That: Making Your Own Classroom Tools with AI
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Department Supervisors
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing teaching; Tool showcase; Success story
Sessions.Tools Featured: AI assistant + browser; Google account; live publishing
Sessions.Description:
Every teacher has a workflow that no product quite fits. Mine was grouping students for workshop-model instruction — a task that ate my prep period every week. So I built a tool that does it. I'm a high school physics teacher with no coding background, and I built and deployed it by typing plain-English requests to an AI assistant.

This session is about the shift from using ed-tech someone else made to building the tool your classroom actually needs. We'll open with a live look at two working sites I built this way, including a walkthrough of how a plain-English request becomes a working change on a live website in under a minute. The first is that grouping tool. The second is a physics website my students use all year — notes, practice problems, and interactive simulations.

Then you'll build one. Using only a browser and your Google account — no software to install, no admin rights, no accounts to create — every participant will describe a simple classroom tool to an AI, get working code back, and publish it to a live, shareable web address before the session ends. Think a vocabulary flashcard flipper, a random student picker that won't repeat a name, a lab timer, or a self-checking quiz. Starter prompts will be provided, so no one starts from a blank page, and we'll troubleshoot together as we go.

You'll leave with a working URL you made and a printed roadmap for going further: from single-page tools, to multi-file projects in an AI code editor, to hosting your own site on a real domain.

No coding experience required. If you can describe what you want, you can build it.

Sessions.Title: The Agent That Builds My Curriculum: One Teacher, One Year, Every Day
Sessions.Short Title: The Agent That Builds My Curriculum
Sessions.Audience: Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Directors / Asst. Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Success story
Sessions.Tools Featured: AI agents; course website; PDF generation
Sessions.Description:
Each morning, an AI agent reads my pacing guide, checks where we left off, and proposes the next day's build. When I approve it, it writes the lesson into my course website — notes, slides, interactive physics simulations — and generates tiered worksheets, answer keys, and standards-aligned rubrics as print-ready PDFs. It verifies its own output before handing it to me. I review and approve every day. Nothing ships without me.

Over the past year this has produced a full physics course: units on waves, optics, orbital mechanics, and electrostatics, each with student notes, slide decks, vocabulary and concept banks, equation practice, and differentiated station work for three ability tiers.

This session walks through the whole system. How the agent keeps continuity when every session starts with no memory of the last one. How it decides whether a given day is a graded checkpoint and builds the rubric to match. What the approval loop actually looks like — including the mornings I sent it back three times.

I'll also show where it has been wrong, because that matters more than where it worked. It has swapped labels on a diagram after misreading a coordinate system. It has quietly deleted an existing lesson while editing a file. Every one of those was caught by a human reading the output, and none of it would have been caught by a teacher who had stopped reading.

We'll close on what a district would need to weigh before anything like this touched curriculum at scale: who owns the material, what review actually costs, and what breaks when the reviewing stops.

Sessions.Title: From Read Along to Locked Mode: Practical Google AI Workflows for K-12 Teachers
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Efficiency & productivity; Tool showcase; Success story; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Tools Featured: Read Along; Gemini in Classroom; Google Forms; Locked Mode; Originality Reports
Sessions.Lead Organization: Central Jersey College Prep Charter School
Sessions.Needs / Requests: Participants should bring a laptop or Chromebook.
Sessions.Description:
Teachers need AI training that is practical, grade-appropriate, and safe enough to use immediately. This interactive session demonstrates two Google-centered classroom workflows: one for elementary teachers and one for upper school teachers.

For elementary teachers, participants will explore how Read Along and Gemini in Classroom can support early literacy, lesson planning, vocabulary, differentiation, stories, choice boards, and visual learning resources. The focus will be on helping teachers create engaging, accessible activities while still reviewing AI-generated content for accuracy, reading level, appropriateness, and student needs.

For upper school teachers, participants will follow a practical workflow from Gemini in Classroom lesson planning to quiz creation, Google Forms setup, managed-Chromebook locked mode, and Classroom Originality Reports. The session will clearly distinguish what each tool can and cannot do: locked mode helps manage the testing environment on school-managed Chromebooks, and Originality Reports identify possible source matches; neither tool proves AI use. Teachers will learn how to combine these tools with process evidence, drafts, version history, student explanation, and fair review practices.

During the hands-on portion, participants will choose either the elementary or upper-school pathway. Elementary participants will sketch a Read Along or Gemini in Classroom activity. Upper-school participants will design a lesson-to-quiz workflow with a responsible assessment and integrity check. Everyone will apply a four-part review routine: accurate, accessible, private, and teacher approved.

Participants will leave with grade-band examples, a simple implementation model, and ready-to-adapt workflows they can use for planning, reading support, assessment, and responsible AI use.

Sessions.Title: AI in Action: From Classroom Practice to Educational Leadership
Sessions.Short Title: AI in Action: Classroom to Leadership
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Tool showcase

Sessions.Description:
Artificial intelligence is transforming not only what happens in the classroom, but also how schools and districts think about teaching, learning, innovation, and leadership. This interactive session is designed for educators, instructional and technology leaders, and school and district administrators who want to move beyond conversations about AI and experience its possibilities firsthand.

Participants will begin with a concise introduction to generative AI and emerging trends, followed by practical demonstrations showing how AI can support lesson and activity design, differentiation, content creation, student engagement, productivity, and decision-making. Participants will then engage in hands-on activities using AI tools to address authentic scenarios from both classroom practice and educational leadership.

The session will also explore what effective AI integration looks like beyond individual tool use. Together, we will consider questions relevant to school and district leaders: How can organizations move from isolated experimentation toward meaningful AI adoption? How can teachers and leaders identify valuable use cases, support responsible experimentation, and create an environment in which AI enhances rather than simply automates existing practices?

Participants will also see emerging approaches to AI-powered learning, including an interactive MetaHuman use case being developed at Stevens Institute of Technology that combines conversational AI with a 3D digital human to explore new forms of learner interaction.

The session is planned to include a guest speaker from OpenAI, either virtually or in person depending on availability, providing participants with an opportunity to hear perspectives on current developments in AI and education.

No prior AI expertise is required. Participants should bring a laptop and be ready to experiment, exchange ideas, and leave with practical strategies that can be applied at both the classroom and organizational level.

Sessions.Title: You Have an AI Policy. What's Next? Turning AI Policy into Practice with Traffic Lite
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents; Other
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Tool showcase
Sessions.Description:
AI policies are an important first step—but a policy sitting on a district website does little to change what happens in classrooms.

In this session, we’ll explore the next step: turning AI policy into everyday practice. We’ll briefly examine how rapidly AI is changing teaching and learning, why students and teachers need clear and consistent expectations, and how schools can move beyond simply creating an AI policy toward actually implementing it.

Participants will see a live demonstration of Traffic Lite, a tool that embeds AI usage expectations directly into Google Classroom. We’ll explore how schools can customize AI usage scales, communicate expectations at the assignment level, manage policies across teachers and groups, and use implementation data to better understand how AI guidance is being applied across a school or district.

Along the way, we’ll consider an important question: What does effective AI policy implementation actually look like in the classroom? We’ll discuss how simple, consistent guidance can help move the conversation away from policing AI use and toward greater transparency, AI literacy, and thoughtful decision-making by both teachers and students.

Finally, we’ll look beyond policy compliance and consider the bigger goal: using clear AI expectations as a foundation for more thoughtful, AI-forward teaching and learning. Participants will explore several practical strategies for designing learning experiences that emphasize process, authentic learning, student reflection, and higher-order thinking in an AI-powered world.

Participants will leave with a simple framework for moving from AI policy to implementation and, ultimately, AI-forward teaching and learning, along with practical ideas they can immediately bring back to their schools and districts.

Sessions.Title: Closing the Loop: A Hands-on Sandbox with Apple Intelligence and Gemini Notebook
Sessions.Short Title: Closing the Loop: Apple Intelligence & Gemini Notebook
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Building Administrators
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing teaching; Efficiency & productivity; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Needs / Requests: Participants bring a fully charged laptop, tablet, or smartphone.
Sessions.Description:
What exactly is a "closed-loop" AI system, and how does it change classroom workflows? In this highly interactive, BYOD workshop, educators and administrators will step away from basic chatbot prompts to explore ecosystem-level AI environments: Apple Intelligence and Google Gemini Notebook. These cross-curricular platforms continuously leverage user data context to automate, refine, and adapt learning workflows in real time.

Participants will spend more than half of this session actively alternating roles between "Teacher" and "Student" across two extended, 10-minute hands-on sandbox challenges. In the Apple Intelligence block, you will evaluate system-wide context features, experiencing how writing tools, smart triage, and native text manipulation dynamically adjust across everyday apps without breaking your workflow. In the Gemini Notebook block, you will experience how to build hallucination-free, source-grounded study environments, generating automatic audio summaries and interactive guides localized strictly to your curriculum uploads.

Beyond practical application, we will tackle the critical security architecture behind these ecosystems. We will address student data privacy by analyzing how school-managed environments protect institutional information, enforce FERPA compliance, and block AI model training. We will directly contrast Apple's hardware-isolated Private Cloud Compute with Google's cloud-based enterprise guardrails, giving you a clear administrative framework to bring back to your district.

By the conclusion of this session, participants will achieve the following learning objectives:

1.        Define the mechanics of a closed-loop AI ecosystem and understand how persistent context streamlines multi-step tasks.

2.        Build localized, secure learning modules using Gemini Notebook and execute system-wide text refinements using Apple Intelligence.

3.        Critically evaluate data privacy features like local processing, zero-data retention, and training lockouts to ensure district safety compliance.

Please bring a fully charged laptop, tablet, or smartphone to actively participate in the hands-on lab blocks.

Sessions.Title: Beyond the Prompt: What Does AI Literacy Actually Look Like in K-12 Education?
Sessions.Short Title: Beyond the Prompt: AI Literacy in K-12
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents; Other
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Efficiency & productivity; Success story; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Description:
AI is showing up in more and more classrooms, but knowing how to use an AI tool does not necessarily mean that a student or teacher is AI literate. As educators, we are still figuring out what students need to know, what teachers need to understand, and where AI fits into good teaching.
     In this session, we will take a practical look at what AI literacy can mean in a K–12 setting. We will start by talking about what AI literacy looks like beyond simply knowing how to write a prompt or use a chatbot. Participants will then work through several classroom situations that involve AI and consider what they would do as the teacher, what students would need to know, and what questions should be asked before using AI.
     Throughout the session, we will look at some of the issues that come up when AI is used in schools, including inaccurate information, bias, privacy, academic integrity, student independence, and the impact AI can have on actual learning. We will also talk about the difference between using AI because it is available and using it because it serves a clear purpose.
     This will be an interactive session, so participants should expect to talk, share ideas, and work through scenarios rather than sit through a traditional presentation. The examples will be applicable across grade levels and subject areas, and you do not need to be an AI expert to participate.
     By the end of the session, participants will have a better sense of what AI literacy can look like in their own setting and a practical way to evaluate different uses of AI with students. Most importantly, participants will leave with questions and strategies they can take back to their classrooms, schools, and conversations with colleagues as they continue to figure out what AI should look like in education.

In this 50 minute session, Director of Technology Mike Sammartano walks through tools in daily use. On the instructional side, these include classroom utilities teachers asked for, science simulations built around the curriculum, and a social story generator for special education. On the administrative side, they include a live staff directory and a searchable family FAQ. You'll see how an idea moves from a teacher's request to a working tool, what runs on local hardware versus in the cloud and why, and how the district handles student privacy, security, and long-term maintenance. You'll leave with a practical starting workflow, a realistic picture of cost and staffing, and a set of questions to bring back to your own team. No coding background required.

Sessions.Title: Agentic AI in the Classroom: Conversations That Deepen Learning
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Tool showcase
Sessions.Lead Organization: Northern Highlands Regional High School District
Sessions.Description:
What happens when students can question an idea, defend a claim, practice a conversation, and receive a follow-up question in real time? This interactive session explores how teachers can design AI agents that engage students in purposeful dialogue rather than simply provide answers.

Participants will experience two approaches to student-facing AI conversations: Brisk Boost activities that guide students through text-based exchanges, and ElevenLabs agents that allow students to practice through spoken conversation. We will consider examples such as a student defending an interpretation of a historical source, explaining the reasoning behind a scientific claim, or practicing a conversation in a world language. In each case, the learning objective comes first. The agent’s job is to ask useful questions, respond to student thinking, and help the student go further.

We will also address practical considerations for classroom use: checking the accuracy of AI responses, setting boundaries for simulated characters or expertise, protecting student information, and deciding what evidence of learning the teacher needs to see. Participants will leave with a design framework, sample directions, and an activity concept they can adapt for their students. No prior experience building AI agents is required; participants who already use AI will have opportunities to refine a more advanced idea.

Sessions.Title: AI, Collaboration and the Learning we Want to Preserve: Building Shared Values Around AI
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Success story; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Tools Featured: Westfield HS AI Learning Group model
Sessions.Description:
Artificial intelligence entered schools faster than most of us were prepared for it. As teachers and students began experimenting with increasingly powerful AI tools, we found ourselves confronting questions that went well beyond whether AI should be "allowed" in the classroom. How do we preserve critical thinking when technology can complete increasingly complex academic tasks? What should students still be expected to do independently? How do we distinguish between AI supporting learning and AI replacing it? And how do we build consistent expectations without ignoring the very different needs of individual disciplines and classrooms?
This session will share the story of Westfield High School's work designed to explore those questions. Rather than beginning with predetermined answers, we created a grassroots AI Learning Group that brought together educators from across departments to experiment with tools, challenge assumptions, examine research, and discuss what we wanted to preserve about teaching and learning. That work expanded to include a school-wide student survey, professional learning experiences, student and teacher discussions around content-specific AI scenarios, and the development of practical resources for teachers.
We will share what we learned from both teacher and student voices, including concerns about overreliance, critical thinking, academic integrity, transparency, assessment, and the changing nature of student work. We will also discuss how those findings led us toward shared values centered on Delegation, Discernment, and Diligence, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach to AI.
The goal of this session is not to present Westfield's approach as the answer. Instead, we hope our process, successes, unresolved questions, and resources can provide a starting point for educators considering similar work in their own schools. The session will conclude with time for questions, discussion, and an opportunity to share how other schools are navigating many of the same challenges.

Sessions.Title: AI, Profound Change, and the Future of Education
Sessions.Short Title: AI, Profound Change & the Future of Education
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents

Sessions.Description:
Artificial intelligence has transformed the conversation about the future of education. Across schools and districts, leaders are grappling with the same urgent question: How should we respond? Too often, discussions around AI focus narrowly on the technology itself and overlook the broader, future-focused transformations that will truly prepare students to thrive in a rapidly changing world.

To help address this question, Jerry Crisci, a former Director of Instructional Technology and a frequent keynote speaker on AI and education, has designed a forward-thinking approach to understanding AI’s role in schools, as well as the profound changes that schools are facing as a result of this technology. In this thought-provoking and highly visual session, Jerry will unpack the “big ideas” needed to plan for using AI effectively, then he will ask participants to work collaboratively to complete a "futuring activity" that could inform their vision for the future of schools.

Sessions.Title: Bring One, Leave With Twenty: The AI Administrator Exchange

Sessions.Description:
The big picture: AI can draft an email or summarize a document. But for school leaders, the real opportunity is figuring out how to use it as part of our everyday work.

Why it matters: Administrators are managing more information, communication, meetings, projects, and decisions than ever. AI can help, but only if we move beyond generic prompts and start sharing the practical workflows that are actually saving us time and making us more effective.

What we’ll do: This will not be 40 minutes of slides about what AI could do. I’ll start by sharing several real examples of how I use AI in the superintendent’s office, including preparing for difficult meetings, analyzing policies and documents, developing communications and Board materials, and organizing projects.

Then, the room becomes the presentation.

The takeaway: Participants will be invited to bring something that is working for them: a workflow, GPT, agent, project, prompt strategy, or other practical use of AI. During the session, each participant will draft a slide in a shared Google Slides deck outlining their specific AI Share—what they use AI for, how they set it up, what the workflow looks like, and how it saves time or makes them more effective. By the end of the session, the group will have built a practical AI Administrator Playbook filled with real examples from school leaders that everyone can take back, adapt, and use.

Sessions.Title: Beyond the Transition Plan
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Directors / Asst. Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Personalization & differentiation; Tool showcase
Sessions.Description:
This session and the white paper it is developed from, are focused on providing access to real world learning for students through the lens of transition learning. Making life skills, social skills, community access, and workplace readiness skills part of meaningful, intentional learning for students through AI is the focus of this session. The work celebrates the value that neurodiverse students bring to our larger community and provides teachers and administrators with research-based learning opportunities to consider how to make these student learning goals universally designed.
This is based on IDEA policy, federal monitoring data, and transition literature. Transition planning is broadly established now; the question is whether plans are coherent and executed. This work was collaborative with a district director, parent of an adult with autism and an educational technology firm developing data driven instruction.
This session will engage participants in considering how the AI tool, Spectrum Shepherd, implements Universal Design for Learning and can be leveraged to engage learners in developing life, social and work readiness skills through a range of experiences that help generalize independence across settings. Teachers, supervisors, and directors will explore how Spectrum Shepherd establishes objective, qualitative and quantitative data around some of the most challenging IEP goals to track. We will discuss the role of progress monitoring, data tracking, and active communication and how this can foster a culture of meaningful transition learning beyond the words in the IEP.
This session will begin with an overview of the research behind the AI-based approach to learning and data tracking. Participants will then explore the Spectrum Shepherd platform. We will then review how to use the data from the evidence report in Spectrum Shepherd to communicate effectively with team members in IEP meetings.
The presenter, Dr. Lori Lopez-Lopez, is an educational consultant working with schools, families, and edtech firms to develop neuroinclusive communities that leverage meaningful data for powerful instruction. Dr. Lopez-Lopez is a former case manager as LDT-C, principal, and supervisor of special education.

Sessions.Title: Stop Asking, Start Building: How Students Become AI Builders
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Efficiency & productivity; Tool showcase
Sessions.Description:
For the last few years, the AI conversation in schools has centered on students typing a question and getting an answer back. Schools responded with policies, bans, and detection tools. But the tools have changed. Today, anyone can describe an idea in plain language and watch AI turn it into a working app, workflow, game, or website. It's called vibe coding, and it changes the question from "How do we stop students from using AI?" to "What will our students build with it?"

We'll start with a quick tour of how we got here, from the early days of AI to the chatbots of the last few years to the creation era we're entering now. Then we'll look at what this shift means for the jobs our students are headed toward. More than half of the job postings asking for AI skills are now outside tech, in fields like healthcare, marketing, and the trades, and those roles pay about 28% more. Employers want people who can build with AI to solve real problems, not just ask it questions.

Then it's your turn. Bring a laptop and an idea, because you'll spend the final part of the session building a real, working app, no coding experience required. You'll leave with something you made yourself, a clear picture of what AI building looks like for students, and practical next steps for bringing it back to your classroom, school, or district.

Sessions.Title: From Static to Interactive: Using AI to Reimagine Old Lessons
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Department Supervisors
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation
Sessions.Lead Organization: Ramapo-Indian Hills Regional High School District
Sessions.Needs / Requests: Participants bring one file from their own classroom.
Sessions.Description:
This session teaches teachers how to turn content they already have — an old slideshow, a worksheet, a review packet — into something students click through, play, or navigate, rather than just read or watch. The core skill is learning to direct an AI tool with your own material as the starting point: instead of asking it to generate a lesson from scratch, you feed it something you've already built and tell it what kind of interactive experience to turn it into.

Teachers will see this in action first through a gallery of real classroom examples: static lessons rebuilt as click-through explorations, review packets turned into trivia-style games, historical or literary units reimagined as role-play simulations, and decision-heavy topics turned into choose-your-own-adventures. Seeing the transformation before the explanation makes the payoff concrete rather than abstract.

From there, teachers apply the technique themselves. Working with one file from their own classroom, they'll practice writing prompts that specify both the source material and the desired output format — the same two-part instruction pattern used across every example shown. By the end, each teacher will have generated a working interactive version of something they already teach, using free-tier access on the AI platform of their choice.

The session is designed to be low-barrier: no new lesson planning is required, just a shift in how existing materials are prompted. Everything works on a free account, so no upgrade is needed to participate — just keep an eye on your usage limits so you don't run out mid-build; if you do, pair up with a neighbor or shift to studying one of the gallery examples up close instead. Teachers leave with a repeatable formula they can apply to any unit, not just a single polished demo they watched someone else build, long after the session ends.

Sessions.Title: AI Goofus & Gallant: Modeling Better Choices for Students
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors

Sessions.Description:
AI is increasingly part of students’ and teachers’ daily lives, but knowing that AI exists is different from knowing when and how to use it well. This interactive session moves beyond AI hype to examine practical choices educators can make when using AI for lesson planning and instruction.

Participants will explore a series of simple “AI Moments” modeled after the classic Goofus and Gallant format, contrasting productive and less productive approaches to using AI in educational settings. These examples will address common classroom scenarios and provide concrete starting points for discussion. Participants will then work in small groups to create their own Goofus and Gallant AI Moments based on their experiences, questions, and instructional needs.

Groups will share their examples with the larger group, creating an opportunity to compare approaches, surface common concerns, and identify practical ways AI can support—not replace—teacher decision-making. Attendees will leave with a collection of classroom-relevant examples and a framework they can use to evaluate potential AI uses in their own practice.

This session intentionally welcomes educators with a range of AI experience, from those who are just beginning to explore AI to those already incorporating it into their practice. The Goofus and Gallant activity invites participants to examine both the potential benefits and challenges of AI through multiple perspectives, including teacher decision-making, instructional impact, and student learning. Small-group collaboration allows participants to contribute their own experiences, questions, and concerns, ensuring that the conversation reflects varied contexts rather than a single approach to AI use.

Sessions.Title: Suit Up: Building Your AI Agent Superhero Team

Sessions.Description:
Every school leader knows the feeling. The inbox never empties, the follow-ups pile up, vendor quotes wait for review, and the work that matters most, being in classrooms with teachers and students, keeps getting pushed to tomorrow. What if you had a team of heroes handling the rest?

In this high-energy, hands-on session, Evan Abramson, Director of Educational Technology at the Monmouth County Vocational School District and an Education Week 2025 Leader to Learn From, shares the origin story of his own AI agent "cabinet." It's a team of named AI agents that runs every weekday, starting with a 7:00 AM briefing. Each agent has a clear mission: a Chief of Staff who sets daily priorities, a project manager who tracks every follow-up, a research analyst who preps briefings, plus dedicated teammates for cybersecurity, budget and procurement, teaching and learning, and communications. The result? Evan got his time back and returned to where he belongs: in classrooms.

You won't just hear about it. You'll watch it work. In a live demonstration, you'll see the agents "assemble," handing off tasks to one another to turn a single priority into a researched brief and a ready-to-send draft.

Then it's your turn. In Hero Academy, you'll build your first AI agent using a Hero Card template. You'll define its mission, its superpowers, and its kryptonite: the guardrails that keep student data, personnel matters, and final decisions safely in human hands. Templates are ready for superintendents, principals, tech directors, curriculum leaders, and HR, so you can start from the seat you sit in.

Participants will leave with:

A working agent prompt you can use the next morning
A Hero Card template for building out the rest of your team
A practical guardrails framework for responsible AI use with staff and student data
A clear plan for which tasks to hand off first

No coding required. No prior experience with AI agents needed. Bring a laptop, a list of the tasks that eat your week, and a willingness to get your time back.

Your superpower was never answering email. Let's build the team that lets you be the hero your schools need.

Sessions.Title: Don't Wait for 2027: One Project to Address the Proposed Computer Science Standards
Sessions.Short Title: One Project for the Proposed CS Standards
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Department Supervisors
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Success story
Sessions.Description:
This session provides an overview of implementing artificial intelligence in the classroom in accordance with New Jersey’s proposed Computer Science, Innovation, and Society standards (NJSLS-CSIS), anticipated to take effect in September 2027. The current New Jersey Student Learning Standards for Computer Science and Design Thinking (2020) remain in effect until that time. The proposed standards do not require a separate K–12 artificial intelligence course. Artificial intelligence is addressed within 8.1 Algorithms and Programming, 8.1 Data and Artificial Intelligence, and 8.3 Digital Tools.

Participants will review the proposed standards, with attention to where artificial intelligence appears, how the 2027 draft differs from the 2020 standards, and how existing classroom practice can address both. The facilitator will then present a student project designed to address those strands: a twelve-node branching narrative constructed on a linked Google Slides template. The project graph functions as an algorithm, and each student choice operates as a conditional. Students decompose a problem into nodes, determine when the use of an artificial intelligence tool is appropriate, evaluate generated output, and distinguish student-created work from AI-generated content.

Following the demonstration, participants will begin building with the template. A laptop and a Google account are required. For at least twenty-five minutes, participants will complete and adapt the activity for their own subject areas, grade bands, and classroom constraints, and will leave with a working copy for use with students. The project is designed to be taught under the 2020 Computer Science and Design Thinking standards and to remain aligned with the proposed computer science standards in 2027.

Sessions.Title: Beyond “Can I Use AI?”: A Practical, Schoolwide Model for AI Literacy and Responsible Use
Sessions.Short Title: A Schoolwide Model for AI Literacy
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Department Supervisors; Other
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Success story; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Description:
As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in students’ academic and everyday lives, schools are grappling with questions that extend beyond which AI tools to allow: What do students need to understand in order to use AI responsibly? How do we establish clear expectations without creating one rule for every classroom and assignment? And how can AI policy reinforce, not replace, education, critical thinking, and academic integrity?

This session will share Northern Highlands Regional High School’s approach to answering these questions through a schoolwide model that combines information and AI literacy instruction with practical guidelines for responsible AI use.

The instructional framework begins with foundational information literacy: navigating academic databases, evaluating websites and online sources, and determining which sources are appropriate for different information needs. Students then apply these critical habits to information encountered in their everyday lives, including, for example, evaluating health and medical claims on social media. Most recently, this framework has expanded to include an introductory AI literacy curriculum for incoming freshmen. Rather than beginning with rules about when students may or may not use AI, instruction begins with understanding on a very basic level what generative AI is, how it produces an answer, why AI-generated information can sound authoritative while being inaccurate, and explores its strengths, limitations, and appropriate uses.

Alongside this curriculum, Northern Highlands developed new AI Use Guidelines for students, educators, administrators, and families. A “red, yellow, green light” model preserves teacher autonomy by allowing teachers to establish the level of AI use permitted for individual assignments, while schoolwide expectations address transparency, citation, and AI disclosure. Importantly, educators are expected to model the same transparency and ethical AI use expected of students by acknowledging their own use of AI.

Participants will see examples from both the curriculum and guidelines, and explore an adaptable framework for approaching AI literacy, policy, and academic integrity as interconnected initiatives. Designed for educators at any level of AI familiarity, the session will provide concrete instructional ideas, policy considerations, and a model participants can adapt to their own school communities.

Sessions.Title: Can AI bring Tier 3 supports into Tier 1 math instruction?

Hear a teacher’s perspective on how she’s integrating AI into her math classroom, and leave this session understanding exactly how to effectively differentiate instruction every day in response to student thinking – making Tier 2 and 3 levels of support a reality in Tier 1 instruction.

Sessions.Title: More Ways to Make Music: Creating & Teaching with AI

Sessions.Description:

In this interactive session, participants will explore how AI music tools can complement human creativity, musical knowledge, and instructional practice while opening new possibilities for educators across disciplines.
Using Suno as the primary demonstration platform, participants will discover how music can be generated and shaped through natural language, musical terminology, original lyrics, singing, humming, and existing audio recordings. We will examine how specific creative directions—including instrumentation, tempo, rhythm, arrangement, vocal style, and song structure—can influence AI-generated productions. Participants will also explore workflows for developing musical ideas, reimagining existing material, and refining generated results through critical listening and thoughtful revision.
The session will then shift from music creation to educational application, demonstrating how AI-generated music can serve as a vehicle for teaching vocabulary, reinforcing academic concepts, exploring themes, and supporting retention across subject areas. Real classroom examples will illustrate how music can make instructional content more accessible and engaging, even for educators without formal musical training.
Throughout the session, participants will collaborate to develop musical prompts, experiment with creative choices, listen to generated results, and refine their ideas. Discussions will encourage participants to consider the relationship between AI and musicianship, the importance of human creative direction, and opportunities for meaningful classroom integration.
Whether you are a music educator, classroom teacher, or instructional leader, this session offers an approachable introduction to AI music creation and practical ideas for incorporating it into teaching and learning. No musical training or previous experience with AI music tools is required. Sessions.Title: Bridging the Data Divide: How Teachers and Administrators Unlock Efficiency with Gemini Notebook and Sheets

For supervisors and administrators, Gemini Notebook provides a powerful workspace to aggregate qualitative and quantitative reports, synthesize department-level trends, and draft polished executive summaries for leadership meetings. Together, we will demonstrate how these integrated Google tools foster a shared language around data, improve institutional data literacy, and reclaim precious planning hours for high-impact decision-making. Whether you are a classroom educator looking to simplify your assessment workflow or an administrator seeking to build an efficient, data-informed culture across your building, this presentation offers practical, privacy-conscious strategies you can implement immediately to turn data analysis into a collaborative success story.

Sessions.Title: Sparking Creativity and AI Literacy through Learning Lab Challenges

Sessions.Title: 8-Bit Literacy
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Success story

Sessions.Description:
Tired of sifting through endless AI tools and apps that promise personalization but are hard to actually use? Build your own! It’s easier than you think.

In this beginner-friendly workshop, you’ll learn a few specific prompting strategies that turn a chatbot into your personal game designer. Together, we’ll create retro 8-bit arcade games aimed at the exact skills your students are working on, from syllables and short vowels to whatever your class needs next. No coding required.

We’ll start by looking at what your students need and describing those skill gaps in a way a chatbot can use, without sharing any student information. From there, you’ll see how a short, well-written prompt can produce a playable game in minutes, and how a few smart follow-ups can shape the look, the sounds, and the level of challenge.

Then we’ll put down the laptops and pick up the Makey Makeys! Using foil, Play-Doh, pencil graphite, and whatever’s in the cardboard bin, you’ll design and prototype a controller that makes your game truly hands-on: a pie-tin drum for tapping out syllables, lily pads for hopping to the right vowel, or something your students would never expect. We’ll talk about designing for small hands, testing with real kids, and why the controller is where screen time turns into active learning.

You’ll leave with a working video game, a controller prototype, and a simple prompt framework (skill, learner, look and feel, controller) for building the next game whenever a new need comes up.

Sessions.Title: Outwit, Outplay, Outlast: AI Strategies for Classroom Survival

Sessions.Title: Pump Up the Jam: Elevating Elementary Creativity Alongside Artificial Intelligence

Sessions.Title: Scaling AI Fluency: Frameworks for Moving K-12 Learners Beyond Basic AI Awareness
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching
Sessions.Description:
As generative AI tools mature, educational discussions are rapidly shifting from initial policy and plagiarism concerns to long-term student preparedness. While many schools have introduced basic AI Literacy—teaching students what AI is, how algorithms work, and basic safety/ethics rules—this level of understanding is no longer sufficient for post-graduation success. Modern higher education and modern industries require AI Fluency: the ability to seamlessly, critically, and ethically leverage AI tools to augment decision making, streamline workflows, and synthesize complex information.

While AI Literacy is knowing about AI; AI Fluency is knowing how to think alongside AI. Fluency encompasses:
1) Iterative Problem Solving: Shifting from single-prompt queries to multi-turn, collaborative refinement.
2) Critical Evaluation & Epistemic Vigilance: Developing the discernment to detect bias, hallucinations, and logical gaps in AI-generated output.
3) Contextual & Discipline-Specific Application: Knowing when to use AI, which tool to leverage, and when to step in as the human-in-the-loop.

This session will bridge the gap between high-level workforce trends and day-to-day K-12 classroom practice. Rather than focusing solely on tech tools, the session provides educators and administrators with a pedagogical roadmap. Attendees will examine how to utilize fluency benchmark indicators and redesign learning tasks to promote higher-order thinking (evaluating and creating) in an AI-saturated world, ensuring students graduate with the adaptable skills required in college and modern AI-augmented careers.

Sessions.Title: Brain First, Bot Second: AI and Reading Instruction That Keeps Kids Thinking
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation
Sessions.Description:
When students use AI first, they often turn in polished work they can’t explain, defend, or even remember. By designing curriculum that encourages students to think first, then turn to AI, we can increase learning and teach students how to have a healthy relationship with technology. In this session, based on the book AI and Reading Instruction (Routledge, 2026), written by Mary Ehrenworth and session presenter Philip Seyfried, you’ll learn how to sequence instruction so that AI deepens students’ thinking.

We’ll connect the latest neuroscience to John Hattie’s research, which places feedback among the most powerful influences on learning, and shows that feedback works only when students have done enough thinking for it to land on. We’ll also draw on Tyrone Howard’s work on culturally responsive teaching and the stance of the warm demander, a teacher who pairs deep care with high expectations and doesn’t let students off the hook.

Then we’ll move into practice. You’ll experience a Brain-first reading routine as a learner. You’ll wrestle with a text on your own, notice where your understanding breaks down, use your own fix-up strategies, and only then bring in AI as a thinking partner. We’ll look at structured AI partnerships, where teachers set up both the chatbot and the students to support metacognition. We’ll also look at prompts that help readers build richer inner conversations with texts. Together we’ll think through the harder question of when it makes sense to lighten cognitive load on purpose, for example for multilingual learners or students for whom print is a barrier, and what to watch for when you do.

By the end of the session, you will be able to:
-Explain the Brain-first principle and the research behind it in plain language
-Design reading tasks that sequence independent thinking before AI support
-Set up chatbot prompts that give warm, demanding feedback and strengthen metacognition
-Decide when and for whom reducing cognitive load supports learning

Come ready to read, think, and try things out. You’ll leave with routines and prompts you can use the next day, plus a framework for every AI decision that follows. No prior AI experience is needed.

Sessions.Title: Vet Your Vendors: Ensure Compliance and Accessibility Prior to Purchase
Sessions.Audience: Tech Coaches; Technology Directors; Department Supervisors; Building Administrators; Directors / Asst. Superintendents; Superintendents
Sessions.Strands: Efficiency & productivity; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Co-Presenter Details: Dr. Lori Lopez-Lopez (Educational Consultant) @ Intella Consulting Associates
Sessions.Description:
As ed-tech vendors' AI evaluations of WCAG compliance increase, genuine human auditing and oversight in the procurement process become crucial. Students with disabilities and the teachers supporting them are often left out of consideration during the adoption of educational technology. This unsettling fact can surface months later in a classroom or an IEP meeting. Anticipating challenges by building structures and processes that put inclusivity at the front of decision-making creates a culture of engagement while ensuring compliance and data behind every decision. This session gives leaders a practical protocol for vetting educational technology tools before purchase in alignment with the forthcoming compliance deadlines under DOJ’s ADA Title II digital accessibility rule. We will cover how to read a VPAT critically, developments in WCAG compliance, and how to differentiate technical compliance vs. student usability. Leave with a procurement checklist, vendor questions, and a pilot-testing template.

Why does this topic matter now?

The Department of Justice's ADA Title II rule requires public school districts' web content and apps, including those provided by vendors, to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. DOJ pushed the first compliance date back to April 2027, but contracts signed this year will still be in use when it arrives, and the compliance deadline for smaller public entities is 2028. Districts that build accessibility into purchasing now avoid replacing tools and/or retraining costs later.

Learning objectives/Participants will be able to:
(1) Read a vendor's VPAT or accessibility conformance report and spot vague or incomplete claims.
(2) Tell the difference between technical accessibility (screen readers, captions, keyboard navigation) and usability for students with learning, attention, and executive functioning needs.
(3) Build accessibility review into their district's existing procurement and pilot process.

Participants will inspect results, identify limitations, and outline one useful workflow for their own setting, including its access requirements and a human review step. Sessions.Title: Guardrails for AI
Sessions.Audience: Teachers; Tech Coaches
Sessions.Strands: Enhancing learning; Enhancing teaching; Personalization & differentiation; Managing misuses & risks
Sessions.Lead Organization: Northern Valley Regional High School District
Sessions.Co-Presenter Details: Jen Glick (Tech Coach & Social Studies Teacher) @ Northern Valley Regional High School District
Sessions.Description:
Should a 9th grader and a 12th grader use AI the same way? Most teachers sense the answer is no, but few of us have a clear framework for why, or for what to do instead.This hands-on session gives high school teachers a practical approach to matching AI use to student readiness.

We begin with a simple premise: students who haven’t yet built a skill can’t judge whether AI is doing it well. For freshmen and sophomores, that means AI works best as a coach and scaffold, used inside structures the teacher designs, while core skills like drafting a thesis and analyzing a source stay firmly the student’s own. For juniors and seniors, AI can become a research partner, a devil’s advocate, and even an object of critique, as long as students verify claims, document their choices, and can defend their work without the tool.

The goal of this session is to understand when “guardrails” need to be up for students utilizing AI.  Completely avoiding AI can be a challenge on its own, so we will work together to discover the ways students can use it in an appropriate manner.  We will begin with an overview of what type of AI use is appropriate for which grade level, and then give teachers the opportunity to transform or create a lesson that allows students to work with AI, without allowing it to do the thinking for them.

Sessions.Description:
Hi there! I hope this session description finds you well. 👋

In today’s fast-paced, ever-evolving digital landscape, AI isn’t just a tool. It’s a partner. A collaborator. A journey. But here’s the thing: not all output is created equal. And honestly? That’s okay.

In this session, we’ll delve into the nuanced, multifaceted world of AI-assisted writing. Together, we’ll unpack what makes content truly resonate, and learn to find the load-bearing argument hiding beneath the fluff. This isn’t just a session. It’s a transformation.

Whether you’re a seasoned professional or a curious newcomer, you’ll walk away with:

✨ Clarity — because words matter.
🚀 Confidence — because you deserve it.
💡 Craft — because the real magic happens in the details.

Not because AI is bad. Not because humans are better. But because great writing lives at the intersection of both. Let that sink in.

Now, you might be thinking: “Isn’t this session itself a little sloppy?” You’re absolutely right to push back on that, and it’s a great question! That’s exactly the kind of critical thinking we’ll be fostering.

No fluff. Just real, actionable insights to seamlessly elevate your work.

Meetups.Name: Local AI For Schools: AI That Never Leaves Campus
Meetups.Description: Every time a teacher pastes an IEP note or a student essay into a cloud chatbot, that data leaves the building. This session shows you how to keep it inside. We’ll set up large language models that run entirely on school hardware, with no internet connection, no third-party servers, and no student information drifting into someone else’s training data. You’ll see which open models are good enough for real classroom work, what kind of machine you actually need, and how to pitch it to the IT director who has said no to everything else. Bring your privacy questions. Leave with a working setup.

Meetups.Name: How To Build a Team of AI Agents: AI Harnesses for Educators
Meetups.Description: One AI assistant is a tool. Ten of them working together is a staff. This session goes inside agentic teams, where you assign roles, set goals, and let a crew of AI agents divide up the work. We’ll use Paperclip, an open-source harness that gives agents org charts, budgets, goals, governance, and audit logs in a single self-hosted app, and lets you pause, reassign, or shut down any agent at any time. You’ll watch a team of agents tackle a real school task live, then talk honestly about what to delegate, what to supervise, and what should never be handed off at all.

Meetups.Name: Lights, Camera, AI: Video Generation and Digital Storytelling
Meetups.Description: Seeing used to be believing. Your students already know that’s over. This session hands you the director’s chair: we’ll generate short films, clone a voice (our own, with permission), and build a scene that never happened, all in under an hour. Then we flip it. How do you teach students to spot a fake, question a viral clip, and tell powerful stories with these tools without deceiving anyone? You’ll leave with classroom-ready projects on digital storytelling and media literacy, plus a new appreciation for how easy this has become.
